To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the kinetics of IRI release is altered in the genetically obese obob and DBH mice and in the GTG obese mice but not in Acomys cahirinus.
the kinetics of IRI release in response to a glucose challenge is altered in obob, GTG and DBM mice.

the kinetics of immunoreactive (IRI) insulin release in response to intraperitoneal glucose stimulation in obob and gold thioglucose obese mice are similar to each other, different from the response of Acomys cahrinus, and that intravenous glucose stimulation results in a rapid release of IRI in obob and Gold thioglucose obese animals.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the kinetics of immunoreactive IRI release in obese hyperinsulinemic rodents.
the kinetic aspects of immunoreactiv insulin release in genetically and experimentally obese animals.
the study of the kinetics of insulin release in obese animals with a special interest in the possible existence of a "first phase" of insulin release in the diabetic state.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the kinetics of IRI release are different in the various obese hyperglycemia models, but that there are some common features, such as the rapidity of the initial response.
the hyperinsulinism of the obese hyperglycemia syndrome is not a consequence of the elevated plasma glucose levels, but is a consequence of the obesity itself.

the obese hyperglycemia in obob and other obese hyperglycemics is not due to a generalized defect of insulin release but rather to a defect of insulin release in response to a specific stimulus, i.e., the ingestion of food.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the obese-hyperglycemic laboratory rodent is characterized by a high basal plasma immunoreactive insulin concentration, an excessive insulin release in response to intraperitoneal glucose, and a rapid initial immunoreactive insulin secretion in response to intravenous glucose.

the obese hyperglycemia of obob and GTO mice is characterized by elevated basal IRI concentrations and an excessive secretory response to intraperitoneal glucose administration, whereas the hyperglycemia associated with the DBM mutation is characterized by elevated IRI levels and impaired IRI response to intravenous glucose administration.
in obese hyperglycaemic laboratory rodents, there are several types of insulin secretory abnormalities.
The main takeaway from our work is that
obesity is not necessarily associated with a defective response of the pancreas to a glucose stimulus.
the secretory response of the pancreatic B cells is a major factor in the development of hyperglycemia in obese hyperglycmic mice.
the secretory defect in the DBM mice is not a consequence of the obesity per se but rather of the hyperinsulinemia.
